Body

How your mass, bones, muscles and eyes are adapting to microgravity, from launch until today.

Before launch

These scans are your reference: every reading in flight is compared with them.

Baseline scans

  • Bone density (DXA) Done Hip, spine, whole body, forearm and heel · up to 45 days before launch
  • Hip structure (QCT) Done 3D scan for long missions
  • Retina scan (OCT) Scheduled Reference for the in-flight eye checks
  • Body mass and fitness test Done Starting point for your mass trend and exercise loads

Your training plan

Your annual physical assessment sets an individual exercise plan. In flight it becomes about 2 hours a day on three machines: resistive device, treadmill and cycle.

A flight surgeon stays with you in high-risk training, such as spacewalk practice in the pool and the centrifuge.

Quarantine starts 14 days before launch: from then on you only meet people who passed a health check.

Show data as a table

Without exercise, weight-bearing bones lose 1 to 1.5% a month in space. The resistive exercise device (ARED) cuts that loss a lot.

Muscle and exercise

About 2 hours a day on three machines keep muscles and heart strong.

Today's plan

  • ARED resistive device 45 of 60 min · squats, deadlifts, heel raises
  • T2 treadmill 0 of 30 min · harness and bungees hold you down
  • CEVIS cycle 0 of 30 min · heart and lung fitness

Even with 2 hours a day, a NASA study estimated that up to 17% of astronauts may still lose muscle and fitness. Your plan adapts to your results.

Vision

Fluids shift toward the head in space and can swell the back of the eye. Regular retina scans catch it early.

Retina scans (OCT)

Normal

8 µm above your launch value.

  • Retina thickness at the optic nerve (µm)
  • Alert level
Show data as a table

Next scan today at 10:30 UTC.

What is SANS?

Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) swells the spot where the optic nerve meets the retina and can flatten the eyeball. There is no proven prevention yet, and it appears about three times more often in men.

Neck vein ultrasound

In weightlessness, blood flows slower in the neck veins, and clots were found in crew members on the space station. A weekly scan catches it early.

Why my neck?

Without gravity, blood and fluids move toward the head and the jugular vein in the neck widens, so blood flows slower there. NASA research found clots in this vein in some crew members; a portable ultrasound shows them, and the medical team decides what to do.

Your scans

    After landing

    After about six months in space, rehabilitation takes around 45 days.

    1. Days 1 to 3

      Gentle start

      Massage, stretching and assisted walking.

    2. Up to 2 weeks

      Low impact

      Walking in water, cycling and light walks.

    3. Final phase

      Full strength

      Running and heavier weight training.
